slides.title: Definitions Types of brakes
slides.body:
Drum brake
It consist of a metal rotating cylinder (drum) and one
or more surfaces coated with friction material
(shoes). When the driver is braking, the shoes are
pushed towards the drum creating a frictional force
capable of slowing or braking the vehicle.
Disk brake
Positioned inside the wheel, operated
by a hydraulic system that uses the
variation of the liquid inside it to
impart to the pads a force proportional
to that exerted on the pedal.

slides.title: Definitions Oversteer and understeer
slides.body:
Behavior of a car that during curved trajectory tends
to travel a tighter trajectory than the one intended by
the driver. If a sudden loss of adhesion of the rear axle
happens, there is the phenomenon of spinning or
skidding.
Understeer
Behavior of a car during a curve that tends to widen
the trajectory of travel, forcing the pilot to make
correction maneuvers (leave the gas and realign the
steering for a moment) to stay on the desired
trajectory. It is a behavior that occurs more on front-
wheel drive cars when they go through a curve at
speed or in wheel lock case.
DefinitionsOversteer and understeer

slides.title: ABS Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Antilock Brake System
On each wheel of the vehicle there is an encoder
(angular position transducer + phonic wheel) and an
inductive proximity sensor. The ECU calculates the
speed of rotation of the wheel and if it detects the
locking of one or more wheels, it acts to help the
driver.
ABS

slides.title: EBD Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Electronic Brakeforce Distribution
EBDVehicle Subsystems
During braking, the braking load on the different wheels of
the car is not the same. This can cause a possible locking of
the rear wheels which, being more flat, and have less grip
with the asphalt. This could lead to a complete lack of
directionality of the car, that can spin. The brake distributor
avoids this problem, especially when cornering, by
lightening the braking force on one or both rear wheels
avoiding locking.

slides.title: ESC Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Electronic Stability Control
It is also known with the BOSCH commercial name
ESP (Electronic Stability Program) or as DSC.
It is a system for stability control of the car, which
acts when skidding happens, adjusting the engine
power and braking the individual wheels with
different intensity in such a way as to re-stabilize the
car's attitude.
The control unit intervenes both on the power supply
of the motor (reducing its torque) and on the
individual calipers brake, correcting the dynamics of
the car.
ESCVehicle Subsystems

slides.title: TCS (ASR) Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
TCS (ASR)Vehicle Subsystems
Traction Control System (Anti Spin Regulation)
It is an electronically managed system that prevents the
drive wheels of a vehicle from spinning during
acceleration. This system is useful in case of critical
conditions (rain / ice), more generally in case of loss of
traction of a wheel. The system identifies the wheel
spinning through sensors placed on all wheels and thanks
to an electronic processor which, processing the acquired
data, intervenes on some variables, which are different
according to the type of control of the system:
- Systems that acts on the brake
- Systems that acts on the engine power supply

slides.title: HH Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
HHVehicle Subsystems
Hill Holder
In the case of starting from a standstill on a hill, it
prevents the vehicle from rolling backwards, in the time
that passes between the release of the brake and the
actual start.

slides.title: Alernators and SAM Vehicle subsystems
slides.body:
Alernators and SAMVehicle subsystems
The alternator has the function of keeping the battery charged, which is necessary to start the engine and to
power all the electrical functions on board. Since there is no way to store electricity in alternating current, there is
a rectifier bridge that has the function of transforming it into direct current and thus allowing its accumulation.
In the automotive field, the concept of SAM (Smart Alternator) was introduced, which differs from the classic
alternator because it is able to vary the power subtracted from the engine according to the running state of the
vehicle.

slides.title: Starter motor Vehicle subsystems
slides.body:
Starter motorVehicle subsystems
The starter motor is a component of the internal combustion engine, integrated into the starting system of
the engine, which allows the engine to reach a number of revolutions sufficient for self-sustaining. It
absorbs current from the battery to rotate the engine, and it is mechanically connected on the same shaft.

slides.title: EGR Vehicle subsystems
slides.body:
EGRVehicle subsystems
Exhaust Gas Recirculation
The recirculation of exhaust gases or recirculation of fuel gases (in the field of alternative internal
combustion engines) consists in recirculating a "small" part (5-15%) of the exhaust gases by making them
pass through the exhaust manifold to the intake manifold, in order to reduce a part of the pollutants
present in the exhaust gases
This is controlled by the engine control unit via a
PWM signal, allowing the regulation of the quantity
of exhaust gases which are recirculated in the intake
manifolds and aspirated into the engine.
The recirculation of burnt gases, inert gases and
gases that do not participate in combustion, by
decreasing the quantity of mixture useful for
combustion and the power supplied, is made to
lower the maximum temperatures of the cycle, thus
reducing the emissions of oxides of nitrogen (NOx).

slides.title: DPF Vehicle subsystem
slides.body:
DPFVehicle subsystem
Diesel Particulate Filter
A diagnosis and management software continuously monitors the filter to ensure correct operation and
maintenance of the same. The filter in question is combined with a pre-catalyst and has the purpose of
physically filtering fine dust. The system collects the combustible gases in the exhaust manifold and then
conveys them to the catalytic converter, passing through the actual filter, proceeding towards the
expansion tank, the silencer and the outlet.

slides.title: Lambda probe Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Lambda probeVehicle Subsystems
The lambda probe is able to detect the oxygen concentration inside the exhaust gases. Through the comparison
measurement of the oxygen present in the ambient air, measured at the other end of the probe, the quantity of air
in the exhaust gases is indirectly obtained.
Lambda indicates the air / fuel ratio
= 1 stoichiometric combustion 𝝀
< 1 fuel excess𝝀
> 1 air excess𝝀
The probe then transmits as an electrical signal to the control unit which regulates the introduction of fuel and air
into the combustion chamber.

slides.title: Lambda probe Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Lambda probeVehicle Subsystems
Types of lambda probes
- Lambda probe with zirconium dioxide
The outer surface of the zirconium dioxide element is in
direct contact with the exhaust gases, while the inner
surface is with the atmosphere.
- Lambda probe with titanium dioxide
The titanium dioxide element does not generate a tension
like the zirconium. By applying a suitable voltage value to
the titanium probe, a current can be measured in output,
which is related to the oxygen concentration in the exhaust
gases.
- Double lambda probe
The single lambda probe sends a two-stage signal (presence
or absence of oxygen): with the use of only one sensor, the
control unit (ECU) must constantly work on the correction
of the injection values e ignition. The use of two probes
allows to have a more truthful sampling and to increase the
duration of the sustem, as sensors tend to vary their
sensitivity with aging.

slides.title: Catalytic converter Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Catalytic converterVehicle Subsystems
The catalytic converter, known as a catalytic converter
or also a catalyst, is a device mounted on the exhaust
system of an internal combustion engine, which
operates preferably between 180 and 380 ° C. This
element acts as a suppressor of harmful gas emissions,
promoting complete oxidation and reduction of exhaust
gases.
It also contributes together with the silencer to reduce
the exhaust noise.

slides.title: Vehicle Subsystems Catalytic converter
slides.body:
Types of catalyst
- Reducing
It is also called one-way because it acts on the main pollutant. It is used for diesel
engines: a rhodium base (Rh), able to reduce nitrogen oxides (NOx) into oxygen and
nitrogen.
- Oxidant
It is also called Bidirectional, as it acts on the two main pollutants. It is used for
engines with controlled ignition, based on Platinum and / or Palladium, that is
capable of oxidizing carbon monoxide (CO) and unburnt hydrocarbons (HxCx)
- Trivalent or oxiding and reducing
It is also called three-way, as it acts on the three main pollutants. It is characterized by
a first reducing catalyst and a second oxidizing catalyst, is used in petrol and gas
engines with stoichiometric combustion and equipped with control lambda.

slides.title: SCR Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
SCRVehicle Subsystems
Selective Catalyst Reduction
Selective catalytic reduction is a chemical process for the reduction of NOx from exhaust gases.
SCR devices are commonly used in both industrial combustion and automotive applications
(Diesel vehicles).
A liquid or gaseous reducing chemical agent (usually ammonia or urea) is added to the exhaust
gas in the presence of a catalyst. The reductant has a strong tendency to absorb oxygen thus
limiting the formation of NOx within the exhaust gas.
A fundamental point of the SCR process is the catalyst: this must be able to make NO react with
O2 and not NH3.

slides.title: Valve Timing Vehicle Subsystems
slides.body:
Valve TimingVehicle Subsystems
The timing is intended as the optimum opening point of the various valves of a four-stroke
engine and is obtained by synchronizing the camshaft to the crankshaft.
This synchrony is obtained with a chain, belt or with gears.
The timing can be fixed or variable.
Fixed Timing
This type of timing is characterized by a simple type camshaft that has a height fixed, therefore
it does not decrease the various phases of the cycle, and it gives a constant phasing.
It does not postpone or anticipate neither the opening nor the closing of the valves according to
the speed, so with this type of timing the engine has a classic distribution

slides.title: Vehicle Subsystems Valve Timing
slides.body:
Variable Timing
A variable valve timing engine has a distribution pattern that varies with varying engine
speeds, generally aids or special camshafts are used which under certain conditions, or modify
the timing or the number of valves that work, allowing to optimize the performance and
consumption (thus also reducing pollution).
Another reason why you can use this scheme is because it allows a differentiated behavior of
the engine, so that up to a certain number of rpm or electronic setting, there is a "smooth"
engine behavior.

slides.title: Vehicle Subsystems Valve Timing
slides.body:
Types of control
- Camshaft rotation
With this type of control it is possible to move the timing without reduce its amplitude.
- Double toothed gear
In this case is used a gear interposed inside the gear which is moved by the distribution and
has the ability to slide on the distribution shaft.
- Variation of cam effect
The cam acts on the poppet valve and therefore is able to vary the amplitude of the valve
timing and on the opening of the valves.

slides.title: Vehicle Subsystems Valve Timing
slides.body:
- Double cam
Several cams are used to actuate the valves on the same side. These cams have different
profiles, and depending on the situation, thanks to a system interposed between the lobes and
the valves, you will have a less pronounced or more pronounced actuation by the cam
- Rocker arm
Only one cam is used, but a rocker arm is used to actuate the valves. The rocker arm is
regulated by a second lobe system, which allows the increase or decrease of the effect of the
lobes of the distribution system.
- Disengageable cams
The cams that are used can slide along the camshaft, thanks to a piloted system, and allowing
the variation of the timing or the locking in closed position of the valves, causing the engine to
run with fewer cylinders.

slides.body:

slides.title: Vehicle Subsystems Valve Timing
slides.body:
Multiair
Multiair is a valve opening control system in petrol engines and diesel engines, created by FIAT
in 2002, and presented for the first time on a series engine (a FIRE engine) in 2009.
The aim of the designers of the Multiair is to provide, in a cam system, the same flexibility as
camless systems.
In a traditional engine, the cam allows you to assign the valve opening and closing profile.
There opening / closing law is fixed and can be optimized through a variable valve timing only
for a restricted operating range, discriminated by the RPM.
In the Multiair system, the tappet consists of two rigid elements connected by means of a
pumping element containing oil. The pumping element is equipped with a valve controlled by a
dedicated electronic system.
If initially the valve of the pumping element is closed, the tappet will follow the opening profile
imposed by the cam. By opening the pumping element valve at a suitable time (according to
the operating situations and when the throttle control is activated), the tappet will be recalled
by the spring and, consequently, will not come reached maximum opening or the closing of the
same will be anticipated. If in the meantime it is requested more power, the control valve will
close again, preventing more oil from escaping, allowing you to use (if still available) the
remaining profile of the cam, but without being able to regain the travel lost with oil leaking.

slides.title: Definitions Transmission
slides.body:
DefinitionsTransmission
The gearbox is a mechanical component that has the function of modifying the characteristic
of the torque (and not of the power) coming out of an engine, similar to a speed reducer. It also
allows you to select a different gear ratio from time to time, depending on the range the
gearbox is equipped with.
The gearbox allows to vary the ratio between engine speed
and vehicle speed, in order to obtain an appropriate drive
torque for the wheels. In fact, the engine has different
optimal rotation speeds depending on whether it is
necessary to favor, if mileage efficiency (generally at
constant speed), or torque and power (for maximum speed,
pickup, acceleration, climbs, etc.) or under torque (for snow-
covered or low-grip surfaces).

slides.title: Manual transmission vs Automatic transmission Transmission
slides.body: Manual transmission vs Automatic transmissionTransmission

slides.title: MTA Transmission
slides.body:
MTATransmission
Manual Transmission Automated
The robotic gearbox is a type of gearbox for automotive use, also called Robotized Manual
Gearbox and derives from the "robotization", replacement of manual drives with automatic
drives, of a normal manual gearbox. By extension, even gearboxes originally designed to be
operated by automatic actuators but with mechanics similar to manual gearboxes, therefore
with gears that can be coupled with sleeves and synchronizers, are also considered robotized.
The electronic control unit, by means of suitable actuators, provides for the clutch movements
and the selection / engagement of the gears, autonomously. This control unit carries out the
process of detaching the clutch, the passage of the transmission ratio and the subsequent
refitting of the clutch.

slides.title: DCT Transmission
slides.body:
DCTTransmission
Dual Clutch Transmission
It is a gearbox in which there are two shafts connected to two clutches in turn, connected to the
shaft transmission. On one shaft there are odd ratios while on the second there are even ratios:
what happens is a simultaneous rotation of the internal shafts, however only one of the two,
thanks to a clutch, transfers the motion to the transmission shaft. Meanwhile, the other gear
ratio shaft continues to rotate and has the next ratio "ready".
The advantage consists in a remarkable shifting speed.

slides.title: AT Transmission
slides.body:
ATTransmission
Automatic Transmission
The most common type of automatic gearbox is that with epicycloidal rotism. A group of
epicyclic systems in series allow each one to make a gear change by means of the intervention
of brakes which act, depending on the case, on the crown, pinion or satellite carrier.
Automatic shifting is usually achieved by exploiting the pressure of a fluid in a hydraulic
circuit essentially operated by a final speed detector.
A transmission with hydraulic epicycloidal rotism gearbox usually consists of the following
parts:
- Torque converter
- Epicycloidal rotism gearbox
- Actuator

slides.title: AT Transmission
slides.body:
ATTransmission
- Torque converter
It is a device interposed between the engine and the gearbox which replaces the traditional
clutch. It produces a variation in torque at low speeds and during accelerations, but above all, it
operates "at idle" (at minimum engine speed) and it doesn’t transmit torque, if not of a
minimum entity and in any case always conquerable by a minimum brake action.

slides.title: FWD Traction
slides.body:
FWDTraction
Front Wheel Drive
Front-wheel drive cars have front wheels that transmit motion.
Front-wheel drive cars can also be divided according to the arrangement of the engine with respect to
the driving wheels. In fact they can be with front motor (the motor is mainly arranged in front of the
axis of the wheels) or set back (the engine is mostly located within the wheelbase of the vehicle).

slides.title: RWD Traction
slides.body:
RWDTraction
Rear Wheel Drive
A rear-wheel-drive arrangement needs the engine and the transmission to be mounted longitudinally.
The engine torque is transferred to the rear wheels. Usually, sports cars with powerful engines have
RWD.

slides.title: 4WD Traction
slides.body:
4WDTraction
4 Wheel Drive
The vehicle's engine torque is distributed equally on all wheels. In these cases it can also be
called 4 × 4. The traction is all-wheel, which is versatile for traveling on uneven surfaces and
for giving the necessary stability to vehicles, which can be off-road vehicles or cars designed for
those who want to use their vehicle not only to go on the concrete road.

slides.title: AWD Traction
slides.body:
AWDTraction
All Wheel Drive
The traction system is capable of distributing the drive torque delivered by the engine to
both axles and to all the wheels. The driver does not have to do anything to activate the
system. The power is distributed over all the wheels or the ECU automatically assigns the
torque to maintain the traction.
The main difference with the 4WD is that a 4WD transmission sends equivalent power to
both the front and rear axles. An AWD shifts the power between the axles as required.
The AWD is suitable for everyday conditions, is used on some off-road vehicles and for some
high-performance riding. The 4WD is suitable for heavier tack.
